articles.title: Faith review – intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitor
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama. Erin Doherty and James McAvoy both bring their A-game in this startling, involving movie from British writer-director Paul Andrew Williams, whose…
body: We are in a downbeat British town, perhaps somewhere in the London estuary, a place to which a candy factory provides employment. Mina (played by Doherty) is a smart, capable single mum to 9-year-old Jamie (Smylie Bradwell); she works on the production line in cap and hairnet like all the others: much liked by everyone there. She is not fussed by the absence of Jamie’s dad and is perfectly content with hanging out with her friends and her sister (Liv Hill).

Williams shrewdly controls the film’s growing, complex mood: a cocktail of dread, fascination and something else, as if Mina has been made a party to some occult conspiracy that Michael isn’t in any hurry to reveal. He already seems to know something about Mina’s babysitter that Mina herself hasn’t suspected. The film’s central dramatic events then kick the mood up into a higher gear. Mina is passionate, bewildered and Michael assumes the priestly air of someone who has seen it all before and who is either here to help or is some kind of vampiric outsider. The problem seemed initially to be that he was too good to be true. Clearly that isn’t the issue.
points: Toronto film festival: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama.

articles.title: River review – so-so survival slasher offers more of the same and little else
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: strong performances from two experienced scream queens and some surprisingly thoughtful direction can’t elevate yet another stalk-by-numbers horror.
body: I t would be unwise and unfair to expect that Toronto’s genre-led Midnight Madness strand would open with quite the same jolt as it did last year with the record-breaking horror hit Obsession. That film was an outlier in almost every respect, both as it premiered and as it was unleashed on wider crowds, the highest-grossing festival acquisition of all time topping out at over $513m worldwide and sparking genuine Oscar buzz.
points: Toronto film festival: strong performances from two experienced scream queens and some surprisingly thoughtful direction can’t elevate yet another stalk-by-numbers horror.

articles.title: The Housewife review – Naomi Watts is a secret suburban Nazi in an overcooked melodrama
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: the chilling true story of a woman who tried to hide from her wartime crimes gets turned into a strangely inert misfire. The first scene of the 60s-set drama The Housewife is a closeup of a whistling kettle, an early “wink, wink” sign that we’re watching a story where…
body: Perhaps if it had been pitched closer to its adjacently named cousin The Housemaid, as a silly, sensationalist thriller, such heavy-handed decision-making would feel more well-suited. But instead, while some scenes flirt with the idea of something juicier, this is a stuffy and stodgy slab of self-serious, old-school Oscar bait complete with all the shouting, crying, throwing and finger-pointing one would expect. Think overcooked rather than slow simmer.

Strangely handled like a big first-act twist, by ensuring that we don’t hear the husband’s American accent for a convenient while and hoping we don’t spot the very clear signposting, we discover that Hermine is the Nazi and has been stringing Joseph along. She claims that her job was a mere nurse, saving rather than slaughtering, and that by associating her with misdeeds, Joseph is showing his ignorance of what the Holocaust was like to live through (“You do not know war in America,” she tells him). But a story is a story and, in Joseph’s mind, a Nazi is a Nazi especially when he finds new information on what really happened.
points: Toronto film festival: the chilling true story of a woman who tried to hide from her wartime crimes gets turned into a strangely inert misfire.

articles.title: ‘Obsession’ One Year Later: Inde Navarrette and Curry Barker Dish on Memes, How Nikki Became More ‘Flirty’ and Their Wild Ride at TIFF
articles.summary: “Obsession’s” origin story is the stuff of legend. On Sept. 7, 2025, just two days after its rapturously received premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the Toronto International Film Festival, distributor Focus Features offered to acquire its rights for $14-$15 million.
body: “What a difference a year makes!” declared TIFF Midnight Madness programmer Peter Kuplowsky, who moderated the talk. Barker and Navarrette regaled the packed theater with how wild the past year and change has been.

Barker, who’d risen to prominence acting and directing in YouTube videos, opened up about how he wanted to become “a true storyteller” and thus opted not to act in “Obsession,” unlike most of his other work. Meanwhile, Navarrette dished on how she was drawn to the project because it was the polar opposite of the type of work she’d done before in shows like “13 Reasons Why” and “Superman & Lois.”
“I got sent the script because I wanted to do something completely different than I’d ever done before,” she said. “I had this fire in my belly, and I wanted to show people what I could do.”
Navarrette sent in a self-tape for “Obsession” and was convinced it didn’t go well.

articles.title: Watch Brandi Carlile and Bonnie Raitt Duet on ‘Love Me Like a Man’ for ‘Austin City Limits’ Premiere, Plus a Web-Only Bonus, ‘Angel From Montgomery’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: For the season premiere of “Austin City Limits,” Brandi Carlile is officially the one being feted, as the episode finds her formally inducted into the Austin City Limits Hall of Fame.
body: When the hour-long program airs on PBS stations Saturday night, viewers will get to see their joint performance of Raitt’s classic “Love Me Like a Man” as part of a show that otherwise consists of selections from Carlile’s latest album, “Returning to Myself.” You can get a sneak preview of that with Variety ‘s exclusive premiere of the Carlile/Raitt team-up.

But there’s more. Recorded during the taping, but not included in the PBS airing, is a second duet, offered here as a web-only only bonus, with the two singers joining forced for John Prine ‘s “Angel From Montgomery,” which Raitt brought to its greatest public attention in the 1970s. “We miss John and we’re gonna hold him in our hearts right now,” Raitt says in her introduction. Watch it below.

The episode premieres on most PBS stations Saturday at 8 p.m. CT/9 p.m. ET (check local listings). The full episode is available to stream at PBS.org and on the PBS App. All Season 52 episodes, including Carlile’s Hall of Fame hour, will also be available to stream free on the ACLTV YouTube Channel.

articles.title: Gore, gimps and a potty-mouthed magpie: welcome to the Lisbon horror festival where nightmares are a dream
articles.summary: MotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares. Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grail.
body: I f horror happens in the dark, the midnight movie showing was once the perfect way of gauging the genre’s health. But those days may be over. “When we were a film club, our first ever cinema screening was Takashi Miike’s Ichi the Killer in 2003, and it was full,” says Pedro Souto, co-director of Lisbon’s horror-centric MotelX festival. “But you don’t have that many people at midnight any more. I don’t know why.” He’s right: the midnight slot I attend – of the gore-bathed Indonesian kung fu flick Ikatan Darah – is only half full. Only a few appreciative chuckles when meat-cleavers plunge into craniums suggest the old midnight spirit still lives.
points: MotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares.
Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grail.

articles.title: ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Creators Andy and Barbara Muschietti on Late Tim Curry: ‘His Legacy Is Incredible’
articles.summary: More than three decades after Tim Curry originated the role of Pennywise in “It,” his impact is still felt across the franchise and horror fans alike. “His legacy is incredible, and we’re very thankful that sometimes our name pops up somewhere close to his,” Barbara Muschietti, the co-creator of…
body: “It’s a shame. It’s bitter, but we’ll remember him,” Andy says. “We’ll cherish it.”

The sibling director-producer duo revamped the world of Pennywise the Dancing Clown in 2017 with a new adaptation of Stephen King’s “It.” Starring Bill Skarsgård as the shapeshifting antagonist, the film was followed by “It Chapter Two” in 2019. The Muschiettis subsequently expanded the franchise with the HBO prequel series, “It: Welcome to Derry.”

Recently renewed for Season 2, the inaugural season of the show premiered on HBO Max on Oct. 26, 2025, and was set in Derry in 1962, detailing the town’s last encounter with Pennywise prior to the 2017 film. Season 2 will jump back to 1935 and, according to the series’ logline, “centers on the bloody massacre of the Bradley Gang, a group of bank robbers who stop in Derry to buy ammo and end up facing unimaginable horror.”

The Bradley Gang Massacre is one of the interludes featured in King’s novel, which Andy teased the second season will incorporate more of. Production hasn’t yet begun, but the director says creatives are currently working on casting.

articles.title: Russell Crowe Wipes Away Tears at Venice Premiere of Music Documentary ‘What Love Builds’ as Fans Yell ‘We Love You!’
articles.summary: Despite his acclaimed acting career, Russell Crowe has always really wanted to be a rock star. That dream appeared to come true on Friday night — at least for 99 minutes — as he premiered his self-directed documentary “What Love Builds,” about his lesser-known music career, at the Venice Film…
body: “What Love Builds” combines concert footage, archive photos and interviews from the past 15 years. Beyond starring in films like “Gladiator” and “Master and Commander,” the New Zealand-born actor has a long-held passion for music and has performed in bands including 30 Odd Foot of Grunts, the Ordinary Fear of God and, most recently, Indoor Garden Party.

“Revealing and deeply personal, it shows how music and acting are intrinsic and interconnected through storytelling and performance,” the film’s synopsis says, adding that it’s “a rare, deep dive into the inspirations behind this legendary and enigmatic artist.”

The 62-year-old Crowe gained international recognition in the late ’90s for his roles in “L.A. Confidential” and “The Insider” and won the best actor Oscar for his performance in Ridley Scott’s 2000 epic “Gladiator.” He made his directorial debut in 2014 with “The Water Diviner” and also helmed 2022’s “Poker Face” starring Liam Hemsworth and RZA. Crowe’s more recent roles include last year’s critically acclaimed “Nuremberg,” in which he portrayed Nazi leader Hermann Göring, and historical drama “The Weight” alongside Ethan Hawke, which bowed at Sundance earlier this year.

articles.title: Farmer left in abandoned, freezing town without food and water for TV show
articles.summary: Ioan Humphreys said he had "zero idea" about what he was getting into in the survival show.
body: A farmer from mid Wales was dropped into an abandoned American town with no food, water, electricity or tools for a new series.
Apocalypse, which starts on Sunday, sees two groups of strangers attempt to survive in a site usually used to train military, with whatever they can find while competing for limited resources.
Ioan Humphreys, from Carno, told BBC Wales he had "zero idea" what he was getting into and was only told it was a survival show about a month before filming.
The 33-year-old was dropped into the town with nothing but the clothes he was wearing - with temperatures dropping as low as -12C (10F) during the challenge.

articles.title: Bids encouraged to keep famed artwork in the UK
articles.summary: Sir Stanley Spencer is synonymous with Cookham, where he was born, lived and set some of his work.
body: A painting by one of Britain's leading 20th Century artists must stay in the country in the hope that one of its galleries or institutions will buy it, the government said.
Sir Stanley Spencer, who was born and spent most of his life in Cookham, Berkshire, is probably best known for the series of artworks he created on the theme of resurrection.

The Resurrection of the Good and the Bad, finished in 1915, is the first piece exploring that topic and is an "immensely valuable" piece to use in the study of his work, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said.
Bids for the painting, with a recommended price of £450,000, will be welcomed until mid-December.

articles.title: Toronto: Anti-Trumpists Are Suddenly Big Progressive Documentary Funders
articles.summary: Kino Lorber head Richard Lorber told a TIFF panel on Friday “civic-minded citizens” opposed to the current U.S. administration are allowing documentaries to get made and seen in theaters.
body: Anti-Trumpists have emerged as a new and growing source of financing for embattled political documentary makers.

Richard Lorber, president of Kino Lorber, on Friday told a Toronto Film Festival panel on connecting audiences to non-fiction movies that progressive, or politically-oriented, documentaries are drawing on “civic-minded citizens with significant contributions, which allow them to get made and give viewers a chance to go to the theater.”

That theatrical success offered Lorber proof of “a ray of light that you’ve suddenly activated, a sleeper cell of fans who you didn’t know even existed.” mTuckman Media principal Michael Tuckman had his own recent success with the theatrical play for the Oscar-winning No Other Land, which has earned around $2.5 million at the box office, and the sleeper hit Secret Mall Apartment, now at nearly $1 million in cinema ticket receipts.

“For me, it was cathartic,” Tuckman said of Jeremy Workman’s 2024 documentary about artists building a hideout in the middle of a bustling shopping mall, as Secret Mall Apartment went on to outpace expectations with its theatrical release.
